narr: Welcome to English for Engineering I, covering weeks 1 through 4. Let's start with some exercises on quantifiers and vocabulary related to trends and movement.
In this first exercise, we'll look at how quantifiers work in sentences about pollution.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Pollution Quantifiers
data.problem: Pollution affects nearly every one of the world's ocean areas. → There are areas of the world's oceans not affected by pollution.

steps.text: Identify the correct quantifier for each blank space.
Remember the difference between countable and uncountable nouns.
Consider the logical implications of each quantifier choice.

data.result: (a) much; (b) little; (c) Most; (d) plenty; (e) a lot; (f) much (too much salt); (g) many; (h) plenty; (i) much; (j) few (few areas not affected = nearly every area is affected).

narr: Let's examine this statement about pollution. The task is to choose the correct quantifier for each blank.
Remember that 'much' is used with uncountable nouns, while 'many' is used with countable nouns.
The answer for the last one is 'few' because if there are few areas not affected, it means nearly every area is affected.
Moving on to our geography section about deserts. This exercise focuses on choosing the correct quantifiers to describe desert characteristics.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Desert Characteristics
data.problem: In geography, a desert is an area which receives afew / little rain and which loses ba few / a lot of its moisture through evaporation. cMany / Much polar regions can be called deserts, but most of us think of a desert as being a sandy, rocky area with d not enough / few water. eLots / Lot of deserts consist of sand dunes or bare rock, and fmany / much are near mountain ranges, which take away the moisture from clouds. Others are far away from the sea or in other water, so receive gfew / little moisture. Although we might assume that very hfew / lots kinds of life live in deserts, in fact there are ilots / many of plants, animals and insects in these regions. jLots / Many desert plants store water in their leaves or roots, and some desert plants can live for klots / many years. Some desert animals live underground. They spend llittle / a few time in the sun and only come out at night. There are menough / lots of insects, scorpions and spiders as well as reptiles, such as snakes, lizards and tortoises, in deserts. They need to spend nmuch / many hours in the sun to generate body heat, so they have oa few / little difficulty living in high temperatures. However, pfew / little of them can bear extreme sunlight, so they tend to move from one area of shade to another.

steps.text: Choose between 'few'/'a few' or 'little'/'a little' for each blank.
Consider whether the noun is countable or uncountable.
Think about the logical meaning in each context.

data.result: (a) little (rain, uncountable); (b) a lot of; (c) Many; (d) not enough (water, uncountable — few water is impossible); (e) Lots (Lots of deserts); (f) many; (g) little; (h) few (very few kinds of life); (i) lots (there are lots of plants. . .); (j) Many; (k) many; (l) little (time, uncountable); (m) lots of; (n) many (hours, countable); (o) little (difficulty, uncountable); (p) few (few of them).

narr: This exercise tests your understanding of quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns in the context of deserts.
For example, with 'rain,' we use 'little' because rain is uncountable, but with 'kinds of life,' we use 'few' because kinds are countable.
Pay attention to phrases like 'not enough' which can be used with uncountable nouns when 'little' wouldn't fit the meaning.
Now let's move to vocabulary related to describing numbers and trends, which is essential for presentations and reports in engineering contexts.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Brainstorm Graph Words
data.problem: Brainstorm all the words you already know to describe the following graphs: (1) an upward trend; (2) the highest point; (3) a downward trend; (4) the lowest point; (5) stability; (6) fluctuation.

steps.text: Think of various verbs and phrases that describe each type of graph movement.
Consider both common and more dramatic vocabulary options.
Group related terms together for each concept.

data.result: Word bank (standard answers): upward trend — rise, increase, grow, go up, climb, rocket, take off, double, jump; highest point — peak, reach a high (point), top out; downward trend — fall, drop, decrease, decline, go down, slump, plummet, halve; lowest point — bottom out, reach a low (point), hit a low; stability — remain steady/constant, level off, stabilize, stay the same, hold steady; fluctuation — fluctuate, vary, go up and down, be volatile.

narr: When describing graphs, it's important to have a rich vocabulary of verbs and phrases.
For upward trends, you can use simple words like 'rise' or more dramatic ones like 'rocket' or 'plummet' for downward trends.
Using varied vocabulary makes your presentations more engaging and informative for your audience.

data.heading: Problem 4 — Complete the Presentation Extracts
data.problem: Complete the gaps in these presentation extracts, using vocabulary from B.

steps.text: Read each extract carefully to understand the context.
Choose the appropriate word from the brainstormed vocabulary list.
Consider the meaning and grammatical structure required for each blank.

data.result: (1) (1) took off; (2) slumped; (3) recover; (4) improvement. (2) (1) slipped (from 9% to 8% — a small fall); (2) plummeted; (3) rocketed; (4) doubled (€250,000 →€500,000); (5) remained steady. (3) (1) unwelcome ups and downs (fluctuations); (2) fluctuated; (3) holding steady; (4) settle. (4) (1) grown steadily; (2) jump; (3) shot up.

narr: Now let's apply our trend vocabulary to complete these presentation extracts.
Notice how different words can describe similar movements but with different intensities or nuances.
For example, 'slipped' suggests a small decrease, while 'plummeted' suggests a rapid and significant fall.

data.text: If you describe a lot of trends, use a wide variety of vocabulary and be dramatic. Sales rocketed in the third quarter is more dramatic and tells your audience more about the trend than Sales increased in the third quarter, for example.

narr: Here's a useful tip from our materials: using varied and dramatic vocabulary makes your descriptions more engaging.
Instead of always saying 'increased' or 'decreased', try using more vivid verbs that convey the extent and nature of the change.

The week concludes with Test 1, which will assess your understanding of the vocabulary and concepts covered throughout the first four weeks.
